title: Compute Is the Constraint, Not Cleverness
excerptForBlog: We usually decide that problems are hard because smart people have worked on them unsuccessfully for a long time. It's easy to think that this is true about AI. However, the past five years of progress have shown that the earliest and simplest ideas about AI - neural networks - were right all along, and we needed modern hardware to get them working. Historically, AI breakthroughs have consistently happened with models that take between 7-10 days to train. This means that hardware defines the surface of potential AI breakthroughs. It's not so much that AI progress is a hardware game, any more than physics is a particle accelerator game. But if our computers are too slow, no amount of cleverness will result in AGI, just like if a particle accelerator is too small, we have no shot at figuring out how the universe works. Fast enough computers are a necessary ingredient, and all past failures may have been caused by computers being too slow for AGI. We estimate that Brain has around 100k GPUs, FAIR has around 15-20k, and DeepMind allocates 50 per researcher no questions asked. There is good reason to believe that deep learning hardware will speed up 10x each year for the next four to five years. The world is used to the comparatively leisurely pace of Moore's Law, and is not prepared for the drastic changes in capability this hardware acceleration will bring. Within the next three years, robotics should be completely solved, AI should solve a long-standing unproven theorem, and programming competitions should be won consistently by AIs.

lessonTitle: Compute Is the Constraint, Not Cleverness
pullQuote: If the bottleneck is hardware, the winner is whoever buys the most of it first.
leadershipTraits: willing to make dated, falsifiable predictions
frames resource asks through a scientific thesis
situation: In July 2017, OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever wrote an internal document — later surfaced as a court exhibit in Musk v. Altman — making a specific resource argument. He was not writing about algorithms or talent. He was arguing that GPU access was the single variable that would determine who reached AGI first. The stakes: OpenAI's competitive position against Google Brain, FAIR, and DeepMind.
insight:
Sutskever's move here is a classic **constraint analysis**. He identifies the one input that limits all others. His line is precise: 'Fast enough computers are a necessary ingredient, and all past failures may have been caused by computers being too slow for AGI.' That is not a vague claim — it reframes every historical AI failure as a hardware problem, not an ideas problem. The immediate business implication follows automatically: win on compute, or don't bother competing.

He then quantifies the competitive gap with unusual specificity — Google Brain at roughly 100,000 GPUs, FAIR at 15–20,000, DeepMind at 50 per researcher. This is the document's hidden move. By naming competitors' numbers, Sutskever turns a technical observation into a resource gap that demands an organizational response. He also flags a timing window: hardware improving 10x per year for four to five years, while 'the world is not prepared.' That is a classic **first-mover window** argument — the advantage is temporary and the clock is already running.
application: Map your own stack for a single constraint — the one input where falling behind forecloses everything else. Then find out what your best-resourced competitor actually holds. If you can't close the gap organically, the document's implicit lesson is to treat that constraint as a fundraising and partnership priority before the window closes, not after.
